Thanks for the report and the screenshot!

**1. The automatic git pull**

This comes from the **"Pull from git before the first prompt"** setting (⚙ → Settings... → Automation → Git). It is on by default. Before the first prompt of a Visual Studio session it runs `git pull` in the solution's repository, so the agent doesn't start editing code that is already out of date on the remote. It runs once per solution per session, not on every message. Because you had fetched, your branch had incoming commits, so the pull brought them in. They conflicted with your local changes, and the extension then put the conflict instructions in front of your message, which is the text you saw.

If you prefer to pull yourself, uncheck that option and the extension won't run `git pull` again.

To get back to where you were before the pull:
- If a merge is still in progress (`git status` says "You have unmerged paths" / "All conflicts fixed but you are still merging"), `git merge --abort` returns the branch to its pre-pull state.
- Your uncommitted changes were stashed automatically before the pull. Check `git stash list` and restore the `autostash` entry with `git stash pop` if your edits aren't in the working tree anymore. Please don't drop that stash; it's the only copy of those edits.

**2. The `[200~` at the start and `[201~` at the end**

That isn't expected. The extension sends multi-line prompts to Claude Code as a single "bracketed paste", wrapped in invisible start/end markers. In your case the invisible part of the markers was lost on the way, so Claude Code showed them as text. It only happens with multi-line prompts, which is why you saw it here: the conflict instructions made your prompt several lines long.

To track this down, could you tell me:
- Your Windows version (Windows 10 or 11, and the build number from `winver`)
- Your Visual Studio version and the extension version
- The terminal type in ⚙ → Settings... (Command Prompt or Windows Terminal), and whether Native Mode is on or off
- Whether it also happens when you type a short prompt with a line break (Shift+Enter) in the prompt box, with no git conflict involved
- Whether "Disable clipboard" or "Send large prompts as file" is enabled in Settings

I'll leave this issue open for the marker problem.

Short answer: no. It doesn't promise to fix everything. If the pull conflicts, the extension leaves the conflict in place and puts instructions in front of your message so the agent resolves it before doing what you asked. Whether that works depends on the agent.

## What happens, case by case

The setting is "Pull from git before the first prompt" (Automation → Git, on by default). It runs `git pull --no-rebase --autostash` once per repository per VS session, before the first prompt you send yourself. The logic is in `Controls/ClaudeCodeControl.GitSync.cs`.

| Situation | What git does | What the extension does |
|---|---|---|
| Uncommitted edits, no overlap with incoming commits | Stashes the edits, merges, puts the edits back | In native mode it shows "Pulled the latest changes…". Your prompt goes out unchanged. |
| Uncommitted edits overlap incoming changes (likely what happened in #264) | The merge succeeds, but putting the stash back conflicts. Git exits 0 and is **not** mid-merge. The edits are left as conflict markers, and a copy stays in `git stash list` as `autostash`. | Adds a block before your prompt: list the files, resolve them keeping both sides, **don't commit, don't merge-commit, never `reset --hard` / `checkout --`**, drop the autostash only after the work is back in the files. |
| Local commits diverge from upstream and conflict | A real merge is left unfinished (`MERGE_HEAD` exists) | Adds a block before your prompt: resolve, stage, commit to finish the merge, never `merge --abort`, and make sure the autostash got restored. |
| Pull fails without conflicts (offline, auth, untracked files that would be overwritten, etc.) | Nothing changes | In native mode it shows "Auto-pull skipped: …". The prompt goes out unchanged. |
| Conflicts already exist before the pull | No pull runs | Sends the conflict block again on **every** prompt (with "still open" wording) until the tree is clean. |

## Is the agent supposed to fix it?

It's asked to, not guaranteed to. The block tells the agent to read both sides, keep the intent of each, and stop and ask when a conflict is ambiguous. The extension never rolls anything back on its own. The way out is always available: `git merge --abort` for the merge case, or the `autostash` entry for the uncommitted-edits case.

## Gaps this issue shows

1. **Terminal mode gives no notice.** The notices above appear only in native mode. In terminal mode, which the reporter used (the `[200~` markers mean bracketed paste in a terminal), a multi-line git block simply appears in their prompt with nothing explaining it. That's why it looked like text appeared from nowhere.
2. **Pulling just because you fetched is surprising.** Incoming commits after a fetch are exactly when the pull runs. Some users won't expect a "send message" button to change their branch.
3. **The `[200~`/`[201~` markers** are a separate bug in the bracketed-paste path. It only shows up because the conflict block made the prompt multi-line.

If you want, I can tackle 1 and/or 2. For example: show a short note in terminal mode as well, or switch the default from pulling to detect-and-warn.

450	
451	- Purpose: the agent should never start editing a file that is already out of date on the remote. `_settings.AutoGitPullBeforePrompt` (default **true**, Settings → Automation → Git) runs `git pull` in the workspace repository before a user-initiated prompt goes out
452	- **Once per repository per session, not per prompt.** `_autoPulledRepositoryRoot` remembers the repo the pull ran for; `RunAutoPull` takes an `allowNetworkPull` flag and returns early when it is false. Rationale: by the second prompt the working tree normally holds the agent's *own* uncommitted edits, so a pull then is both the most likely to produce an autostash-restore conflict (see below) and the least likely to find anything — while charging every single send a network round-trip on the UI path. Keyed by root rather than a bare bool so switching solutions re-arms it; it does **not** re-arm on agent restart or after an idle period
453	- The flag is set from `GitPullOutcome.PullExecuted` (true whenever the `pull` command itself ran, including when it *failed*) — an offline or unauthenticated remote would otherwise re-pay the full 20 s `GitSyncPullTimeoutMs` on every prompt for the rest of the session. Leftover conflicts found *before* any pull set `PullExecuted = false`, so the session's pull stays available for the next prompt
454	- The local `GetUnmergedPaths` check at the top of `RunAutoPull` still runs on **every** prompt, before the `allowNetworkPull` guard: it is a local `git status`, and a prompt going out over an unresolved tree is worth interrupting no matter who left it conflicted
455	- Repository resolution **never** reads `_gitRepositoryRoot` (v234.0): `TryAutoPullBeforePromptAsync` always resolves `GetWorkspaceDirectoryAsync()` + `FindGitRepositoryRoot()` (a local walk up for `.git`). That field belongs to diff tracking and is only ever assigned by `EnsureDiffTrackingStartedAsync`, which on the send path runs *after* the pull hook — null on the first prompt of a session, and after opening another solution in the same VS it still names the *previous* solution's repository. Before v234.0 the pull used it when non-empty, so the new solution's first prompt resolved the old root, found it already in `_autoPulledRepositoryRoot`, and went out unpulled (measured: one VS process, Devin native in `GOT` then `GenesysAutomations`). Every skip path goes through `LogSkip`, which writes to `Debug.WriteLine` **and** `terminal-launch.log` (Debug output is compiled out of Release, and a skip is silent by design); `ReportAutoPullOutcome` logs the outcome there too. The "already pulled" skip names the repository root, so a stale root shows up in the log
456	- Hooked into `SendButton_Click` (UserInput.cs) and, since v193.0, `CustomCommandMenuItem_Click` (CustomCommands.cs) — both are user-initiated sends. Deliberately *not* into `SendTextToAgentAsync` itself: the automatic senders (build errors, runtime errors, agent-finish follow-ups) must not trigger network I/O or move files under a turn that is already running, so they call `SendTextToAgentAsync` directly without going through either hook. A half-finished rebase is none of those things. On conflict, `BuildConflictPromptBlock` is prepended to `fullPrompt` ahead of the attachment block, listing the unmerged paths and telling the agent to resolve them before the user's own request

466	  | Clean-ish tree, only *uncommitted* edits conflict with upstream | **0** | **absent** | absent | `stash@{0}: autostash` |
467	
468	  In the second row the merge (or fast-forward) already succeeded and it was *reapplying the autostash* that conflicted — and it is the more common case in day-to-day work. Telling the agent there to "stage the resolved files and commit to complete the merge" would commit the user's uncommitted work-in-progress as a merge commit. Version 308.0 is published to the Marketplace (commit `22b5a37`, pushed to master) and issue #264 is closed. I haven't tried it in a running VS (F5); I only checked the individual git commands by hand on scratch repos.

**What changed**
- **No more auto-pull conflicts:** the extension now runs `git fetch` first and checks what's coming in before it merges:
  - **Nothing new:** reports up to date and merges nothing.
  - **Incoming changes touch files you've edited:** this includes uncommitted edits, untracked files, and renames. Nothing is pulled; a notice names up to three of the files and says nothing was pulled.
  - **You have local commits:** git predicts whether the merge would conflict. If it would, nothing is pulled and you get the same kind of notice. On git older than 2.38 it falls back to "both sides changed the same file", which can only over-warn.
  - **Otherwise:** it merges, keeping your uncommitted edits to unrelated files. The old conflict-handling path is still there for anything these checks miss, and for conflicts that were already open.
- **Timeouts no longer repeat:** a fetch or merge that times out now counts as the session's one pull, so an unreachable remote no longer adds a 20-second wait to every prompt.
- **Terminal mode now shows the result:** it appears as a Visual Studio notification bar with a "Turn off auto-pull" link. Before, nothing in terminal mode explained the pull.
- **Translations and docs:** the four new strings are translated in all 19 language files. The README and `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` are updated, and 8 new unit tests cover the new helpers. All 1100 tests pass.

- TUI fullscreen env vars (v31/v32, `GetClaudeCommand`): `_settings.ClaudeTuiFullscreen` (nullable) injects an env prefix ahead of the `claude` command — `true` → `CLAUDE_CODE_NO_FLICKER=1` plus `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_MOUSE=1`; `false` → `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_ALTERNATE_SCREEN=1` (classic renderer); `null` → nothing (CLI default). cmd.exe form is `set X=1 && set Y=1 && {cmd}`, WSL bash form is `X=1 Y=1 {cmd}`. `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_MOUSE` is mandatory whenever fullscreen is on (issue #92): fullscreen rendering enables Claude Code's own terminal mouse tracking, which in the embedded conhost — where the extension already runs a global mouse hook and re-asserts focus — emits a continuous burst of mouse-input escape sequences that Claude's fast-input heuristic collapses into `[Pasted text +N lines]` bracketed-paste blocks, flooding the prompt on launch and on every restart. The extension supplies its own mouse zoom / click-to-focus / paste, so disabling Claude's mouse capture loses nothing while keeping the flicker-free draw. The one casualty is wheel scrolling: with Claude's mouse off, the wheel no longer pages the conversation (per Claude's docs, fullscreen + `DISABLE_MOUSE` keeps only the keyboard scroll keys `PgUp`/`PgDn`/`Ctrl+Home`/`Ctrl+End`, plus native terminal selection of the visible viewport). Wheel scroll restored without re-enabling Claude's mouse (v36, issue #96): the global mouse hook's `HandleMouseHookEvent` now, on a plain (no-Ctrl) wheel notch over the active panel when `IsClaudeFullscreenConhostActive()`, posts `VK_PRIOR`/`VK_NEXT` (PgUp/PgDn) keystrokes to the terminal via `SendScrollKeyToTerminal`. Two gotchas: (1) `ShouldDispatchMouseHookMessage` must let the plain wheel through — it otherwise forwards `WM_MOUSEWHEEL` only when Ctrl is held (zoom), so the plain-wheel case is gated on `IsClaudeFullscreenConhostActive()` there too, or the handler never runs. (2) `SendScrollKeyToTerminal` builds a real `lParam` (scan code from `MapVirtualKey` + extended-key bit) — conhost silently drops a posted key with a zero scan code instead of translating it to VT input (`ESC[5~`/`ESC[6~`). Posted straight to `terminalHandle` (focus-independent, like the Enter path); gated to conhost (`_wtTabBarHeight <= 0`) and the Claude Code / Claude Code (WSL) providers so it never hijacks conhost's own scrollback in the classic renderer or Windows Terminal's native wheel handling. Smooth line scroll (vs. the half-page PgUp default): for *native* Claude Code, `TryEnsureFullscreenLineScrollKeybinding()` merges `pageup`→`scroll:lineUp`, `pagedown`→`scroll:lineDown` (and `shift+pageup/pagedown`→`scroll:halfPage*` to preserve paging) into `%USERPROFILE%\.claude\keybindings.json` — those line-scroll actions are unbound by default, so the wheel had nothing finer than half-page to trigger. With the binding in place each notch sends one PgUp/PgDn (`GetFullscreenWheelScrollKeystrokeCount()` returns 1) for a one-line step; WSL Claude (config lives in the WSL filesystem) and any write failure fall back to a single half-page keystroke. The keybinding file is touched once per session, lazily on first wheel scroll, and merges without overwriting existing user bindings (`AddBindingIfAbsent`).

That host has no bracketed-paste support, so a paste reaches a TUI as ordinary keystrokes. Under it, UserInput.cs (a) forces prompts over the 1 KB threshold onto the temp-file reference regardless of `SendLargePromptsAsFile`, and (b) disables the `DisableClipboardSend` keystroke path so sends stay on the single handle-targeted `WM_COMMAND` paste

enabled, any pasted text is bracketed with a pair of escape sequences,

Bracketed paste mode was added to Windows Terminal in PR #9034.

This only applies when VT input mode is enabled, since that is the way
Windows Terminal currently works.

enabled. That's necessary to prevent any attempts to bypass the
bracketing, but I didn't want to mess with the expected behavior for
legacy apps if bracketed mode is disabled.

confirmed that pasted content is now buffered, instead of being executed
immediately.

Also tested in VIM, and confirmed that you can now paste preformatted
code without the autoindent breaking the formatting.

   - Conhost has its own bracketed-paste mode (microsoft/terminal PR #15155, merged 2023-04-26):
     - When the app enables `ESC[?2004h` with VT input mode on, conhost wraps the paste in its own markers.

The extension supplies its own mouse zoom / click-to-focus / paste, so disabling Claude's mouse capture loses nothing while keeping the flicker-free draw. The one casualty is wheel scrolling: with Claude's mouse off, the wheel no longer pages the conversation (per Claude's docs, fullscreen + `DISABLE_MOUSE` keeps only the keyboard scroll keys `PgUp`/`PgDn`/`Ctrl+Home`/`Ctrl+End`, plus native terminal selection of the visible viewport). (2) `SendScrollKeyToTerminal` builds a real `lParam` (scan code from `MapVirtualKey` + extended-key bit) — conhost silently drops a posted key with a zero scan code instead of translating it to VT input (`ESC[5~`/`ESC[6~`). Posted straight to `terminalHandle` (focus-independent, like the Enter path); gated to conhost (`_wtTabBarHeight <= 0`) and the Claude Code / Claude Code (WSL) providers so it never hijacks conhost's own scrollback in the classic renderer or Windows Terminal's native wheel handling. With the binding in place each notch sends one PgUp/PgDn (`GetFullscreenWheelScrollKeystrokeCount()` returns 1) for a one-line step; WSL Claude (config lives in the WSL filesystem) and any write failure fall back to a single half-page keystroke. The keybinding file is touched once per session, lazily on first wheel scroll, and merges without overwriting existing user bindings (`AddBindingIfAbsent`).
